meta.fix_commit: php/php-src 82f8f31b16a ("Avoid state corruption via bailout", branch PHP-8.0-CVE-2026-109618-109619) - fixes both CVEs together
meta.note: 2026-10-21 rewrite: this file previously described a single-request multipart-stall heap-spray mechanism (byte offsets, FILLUNIT, 149-field spray count) derived from the leaked PoC artifact's own claims. That mechanism did not match the real fix and has been deleted, not caveated. Everything below is grounded in the actual php-src fix commit. See ANALYSIS.md for the full writeup.

vulnerability.root_cause: zend_mm_safe_error (Zend/zend_alloc.c) handled OOM/integer-overflow via zend_error_noreturn + unconditional zend_bailout() - both longjmp-based, skipping cleanup code downstream of the jump point. Fixed by replacing with a hard _exit(1), no longjmp.
vulnerability.cross_request_mechanism: A longjmp-interrupted (producer) request can skip the reset of worker-persistent globals (EG(user_error_handler), EG(exception), EG(objects_store), PG(http_globals)[], PG(modules_activated), SG(request_info).auth_user/auth_password/auth_digest/content_type_dup/current_user). A later, different (consumer) request on the SAME worker process can read these before its own init_executor()/php_request_startup() resets them.
confirmed_consumer_paths: zend_error_zstr_at - reachable via early INI diagnostics (e.g. .htaccess/php_value under mod_php)
php_session_rfc1867_callback - the session.upload_progress multipart hook; confirmed by the EOL-branch fix disabling it outright (if (!PS(rfc1867_enabled) || true))
vulnerability.producer_amplification_vector: main/rfc1867.c's multipart_buffer_headers() previously saved every header line in a multipart part unconditionally - an attacker-controlled single part with an unlimited number of headers costs far more memory inside PHP than on the wire, driving OOM cheaply. Fixed: now only saves Content-Disposition/Content-Type, skips duplicates.
vulnerability.mitigation: No complete generic configuration mitigation (per the PHP advisory). session.upload_progress.enabled=0 closes one confirmed consumer path; fatal_error_backtraces=0 (PHP 8.5 only) closes the strongest confirmed producer path. Preventing worker reuse (pm.max_requests=1 / MaxConnectionsPerChild 1) makes the cross-request consumer step structurally impossible, at a performance cost.

heap_reclaim_technique.note: Separate from the trigger: the fix also hardens how freed memory gets reclaimed. main/php_variables.c now builds $_POST/$_GET/$_COOKIE via a new array_init_singleton() (Zend/zend_hash.c's zend_new_array_singleton(), nTableSize forced to 1) instead of the default dynamically-sized array_init(). This confirms a heap-spray/reclaim step is a real part of exploitation -- it is just reached via the cross-request mechanism above, not a same-request spray at fixed byte offsets. No specific blob layout or offset table is confirmed for the real mechanism; the ones in the prior revision of this file were artifact-specific claims that do not match the fix.

host_indicators.note: 2026-10-21 addition, in response to 'how does this help as an IoC?' for the fpm-worker-recycle-85 pcap specifically: the network signal (9109633) only covers the producer request itself, on the wire, at the moment it's sent -- it does not and cannot show whether that request actually reached the vulnerable longjmp/bailout path, or whether a later request then read the dangling state. The php-fpm error log can show the first half of that directly, which no packet capture can.
host_indicators.php_fpm_log_pattern: WARNING: [pool <name>] child <pid> exited with code 70 after <N> seconds from start, immediately followed by NOTICE: [pool <name>] child <new_pid> started on the same pool. (That is the literal log text -- it does not itself say 'unrecoverable' or name a cause; code 70 is sysexits.h's generic EX_SOFTWARE, reused by FPM for several unrelated conditions too, see false_positive_note.) Confirmed in both reproductions (examples/logs/phpup2026-real-oom-amplification-phpfpm.log, examples/logs/phpup2026-real-fpm-worker-recycle-85-phpfpm.log) to correlate exactly (same second) with the producer HTTP request's own response timestamp.
host_indicators.what_this_confirms: 2026-10-21, corrected after checking php-src directly at the fix commit's parent (670052c): verified sapi/fpm/fpm/fpm_main.c does `if (php_request_startup() == FAILURE) { ...; return FPM_EXIT_SOFTWARE; }` (70). There is no separate 'unrecoverable' vs 'ordinary recoverable' fatal at the engine level -- every memory_limit-triggered fatal (any size) calls the same Zend/zend_alloc.c zend_mm_safe_error() -> zend_bailout(), confirmed by reading that function directly. What exit-code-70 actually confirms is narrower and more specific than 'hit the bailout path': it confirms the bailout happened *during php_request_startup() itself* (which runs the vulnerable main/rfc1867.c multipart-header parsing, before user code runs) rather than later in a mid-script fatal, which is exactly the producer-side precondition CVE-2026-109619's cross-request step needs. Apache's mod_php SAPI (sapi/apache2handler/sapi_apache2.c) hits the identical zend_bailout() for the identical payload but has no equivalent self-exit check, which is why its worker survives the same condition -- see ANALYSIS.md's 'What we have NOT reproduced' section for the full source-level comparison.
host_indicators.what_this_does_not_confirm: That any later request actually read the dangling globals and that exploitation succeeded -- that consumer-side step is in the 'unreproduced' section below and is NOT confirmed by this indicator alone. Treat 'exited with code 70' as 'a producer-trigger candidate fired here, go look at what request immediately followed it on the same worker,' not as 'RCE confirmed.'
host_indicators.false_positive_note: Exit code 70 is sysexits.h's generic EX_SOFTWARE, and php-fpm's own fpm_main.c returns it from several other, unrelated failure points too (config/startup errors, not just a request_startup bailout) -- so in principle it can be reached by other causes besides this specific bug. Correlate with the network signal (9109633 firing on the immediately preceding request on the same connection/pool) before treating it as this vulnerability specifically, not in isolation.
host_indicators.response_shape_caveat: The crash does not reliably surface as an HTTP 502: in the oom-amplification.pcap capture (8.3.6), nginx did return 502. In the fpm-worker-recycle-85.pcap capture (8.5.0, same mechanism), it did not -- PHP had already flushed response headers before the bailout fired, so nginx forwarded a 200 OK with an empty, prematurely-terminated chunked body instead. Don't rely on 502 alone as the host-visible symptom.

reproduced_2026_10_21.note: Own lab, pre-patch PHP 8.3.6 (Ubuntu 8.3.6-0ubuntu0.24.04.12 -- the distro's default .13 build already had the fix backported despite the unchanged version string; confirmed via zend_new_array_singleton symbol presence/absence). One multipart part, 1,400,000 duplicate 5-byte header lines, 7,000,111 bytes wire.
reproduced_2026_10_21.measured_via: PHP's own memory_get_peak_usage(true) -- the metric memory_limit enforcement checks against, not an external RSS proxy (RSS sampling was flat/misleading in an earlier attempt)
reproduced_2026_10_21.memory_limit_sweep: 2M/4M/8M/16M/32M/64M/128M/256M -> hard worker crash + respawn (502, php-fpm log 'exited with code 70', new child PID). 512M/1024M -> clean 200, same worker PID before/after.
reproduced_2026_10_21.gap: Crash-and-respawn at low memory_limit is NOT the survive-with-corrupted-state CVE-2026-109619 needs. See unreproduced section.

unreproduced.note: An end-to-end RCE, or even a confirmed ASAN use-after-free, under whichever producer trigger leaves a surviving (not crashed) worker. Tested PHP 8.5.0 (genuinely pre-patch, built from source) with fatal_error_backtraces=On (default): an ordinary uncaught fatal and an ordinary memory_limit soft-check fatal both survive cleanly, no visible corruption -- expected, since both go through PHP's intact normal fatal-error pipeline. The SAME header-explosion payload that produced 408MB/58x on 8.3 also reproduces on 8.5 (440MB peak at memory_limit=512M) but hits the identical hard-crash-and-respawn pattern below that threshold, exit code 70 both times (FPM_EXIT_SOFTWARE; see host_indicators above for exactly what triggers it in fpm_main.c). This suggests php-fpm's own worker-recycling-on-fatal is an incidental mitigation against the cross-request consumer step, and that reproducing it needs Apache+mod_php (which the advisory specifically names as where RCE was confirmed) rather than php-fpm. Not yet built. Also unconfirmed: which early-init paths beyond php_session_rfc1867_callback and zend_error_zstr_at are reachable in a default configuration. See ANALYSIS.md.

reproduced_85_2026_10_21.note: Own lab, PHP 8.5.0 built from source (genuinely pre-patch -- ondrej/php PPA and packages.sury.org both only distribute the already-patched 8.5.12). fatal_error_backtraces=On (default).
reproduced_85_2026_10_21.ordinary_fatals_survive: uncaught undefined-function error, and memory_limit soft-check fatal -- both: same worker PID before/after, no visible corruption

same_header_explosion_trigger_as_83.memory_limit_sweep_2M_16M_128M_256M: hard worker crash + respawn every time, exit code 70 (php-fpm internal), identical pattern to PHP 8.3

this_artifact_only._note: Literal to the one released PoC (http://jackalsyn.com/posts/phpupAssets/php-up-2026.tar.gz, sha256 0c254d547cac650bfbcb2275e30c2083737520a51a0511646f1fbb7ed60a0d63). VulnCheck independently reports that none of the public PoCs they reviewed have the correct mechanism for this CVE pair -- treat this artifact's own documented technique as unverified, not as a description of the real vulnerability. These strings remain useful only as blocklist-grade IOCs for that one tool/campaign, same caveat as before. 2026-10-21 addition: this CVE pair is now publicly tracked under the name 'php2shell' (searched GitHub directly, found a dozen+ repos using that name, several specifically for CVE-2026-109618/109619) -- this artifact and that public name are the same lineage, not coincidence: the credited original researchers (README.md's own byline) include 'Atlas', and this artifact's full framework (bin/php_up_framework.py) defaults its session ID to that same handle (sid = 'atlas' + 24 random hex chars) when --sid is not overridden. See ANALYSIS.md's 'A wrong theory went public' for why NOT to trust the mechanism description in most public php2shell repos, which repeat this artifact's own (already-retired) theory.

http.sid_prefix_note: bin/php_up_framework.py (the artifact's general-purpose tool, distinct from the simplified bin/poc_trigger.py which uses the fixed all-'a' SID above): `sid = a.sid or ('atlas' + uuid.uuid4().hex[:24])` -- a 29-character cookie value with a literal 'atlas' prefix followed by 24 lowercase-hex characters, used whenever an operator runs the tool without passing --sid. Suricata/Sigma: match `PHPSESSID=atlas[0-9a-f]{24}` in the cookie.

files._note: Three real, non-stripped ELF debug shared objects under deltas/, one per target distro (Debian Bookworm, Ubuntu Jammy, Ubuntu Noble), built from lsphp82 8.2.34 (LiteSpeed's PHP 8.2 package) and used by the artifact's --syms symbol-extraction mode. If any of these exact files are found on disk (dropped by an operator running this tool locally, or staged for later use), that is a strong, literal match -- not a behavioral heuristic.

memory_constants._note: bin/php_up_framework.py's DELTA_CALL_AUTHOR = 0x43EF0, the author's own hardcoded zend_call_function delta, used to derive a default --call address when --dtor is supplied without --call. The file's own comment flags it as 'ONLY valid for Ubuntu php 8.5.4 profile-21' -- an operator targeting any other build must override it, so this constant is a weak signal (absence doesn't mean a different tool; presence in a memory/network capture would mean this exact tool, unmodified, against that one specific build).
